chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Mechanics of Sovereign Debt Sustainability

lessons.title: The IMF-World Bank Debt Sustainability Framework and Its Blind Spots

body.text: A Debt Sustainability Analysis is not a prediction that a country will default. It is a structured judgment call, and its documented blind spots, hidden debt, optimistic growth assumptions, and one-size-fits-all thresholds, have each let a real crisis go unflagged until it was too late.

children.text: The IMF and World Bank do not casually estimate whether a country can pay its debts. They run a formal, standardised process called a Debt Sustainability Analysis, or DSA, every time a country enters an IMF-supported program, undergoes its annual Article IV surveillance, or sits down to negotiate a debt restructuring. Two separate frameworks exist depending on the country: one for economies with real access to international capital markets, and one for low-income countries that borrow mostly on concessional terms. Both produce a risk rating that markets, rating agencies, and restructuring negotiators treat as close to gospel. This lesson takes the machinery apart: how a DSA is actually built, what its standardised stress tests do and don't capture, and three specific blind spots that have each, at different points, let a real sovereign crisis go undetected until it was too late.

columns.label: MAC DSA (Market-Access Countries)
points: Applies to most emerging markets and all advanced economies, including India, Brazil, and Indonesia
Produces a mechanical risk signal (low, moderate, or high) from debt and gross financing need thresholds, which IMF staff can then override with judgment
Central to every Article IV surveillance report and every exceptional-access IMF program

columns.label: LIC DSF (Low-Income Country Debt Sustainability Framework)
points: A joint IMF-World Bank framework for countries eligible for concessional IDA financing, most of Sub-Saharan Africa plus countries like Zambia and Mozambique
Classifies external debt distress risk (low, moderate, high, or already in distress) using a Composite Indicator built from growth, reserves, remittances, and the World Bank's CPIA governance score
Central to G20 Common Framework restructuring negotiations; most recently revamped in 2017

children.text: How a DSA Actually Works: Baseline Plus Stress Tests

Every DSA starts with a baseline scenario: the country's, or the IMF staff's own, projections for growth, inflation, the primary balance, and interest rates, run forward five to ten years using the debt dynamics identity from the previous lesson. On its own, a baseline is close to useless, because almost every finance ministry's own baseline shows its debt stabilising. What does the real analytical work is a set of standardised stress tests layered on top of that baseline, each one shocking a single variable to see how much the projected debt path or gross financing need deteriorates.

stats.label: Growth Shock
stats.context: Real GDP growth shocked one historical standard deviation below baseline

stats.label: Primary Balance Shock
stats.context: Fiscal balance shocked using the same historical-standard-deviation logic

stats.label: Interest Rate Shock
stats.context: A sharp, sustained rise in borrowing costs; typical order of magnitude for EM stress tests

stats.label: Contingent Liability Shock
stats.context: Simulates a financial-sector bailout or bank recapitalisation hitting the debt stock in a single year

children.text: The exact size of each shock varies by country and by which vintage of the framework is in use, but the shape of the exercise stays constant: shock one variable at a time, then combine several shocks, and check whether the debt-to-GDP ratio or the gross financing need still returns to a stable path.

body.label: Gross Financing Need (GFN) Benchmark
body.context: GFN, the fiscal deficit plus maturing debt due for rollover in a year, crossing this level is treated as an early warning of rollover risk under the MAC DSA, even when the debt stock itself still looks manageable

body.text: The headline low, moderate, or high risk rating a DSA produces is not purely mechanical. The framework generates a mechanical signal from the thresholds, but IMF staff retain the ability to override it with judgment, upward or downward, and document why. That judgment call is exactly where politics, staff incentives, and plain forecasting error have crept into DSAs that later turned out to be badly wrong.

children.text: Blind Spot 1: Contingent Liabilities and Hidden Debt

body.title: When Hidden Debt Broke the Official Numbers

events.title: Mozambique's Hidden Loans
events.description: State-owned companies borrowed roughly $2 billion through undisclosed, government-guaranteed loans, arranged partly to finance a tuna-fishing fleet. When the loans surfaced in 2016, Mozambique's official debt numbers were revealed to have missed a debt load large enough to trigger default and a multi-year suspension of IMF support.

events.title: Zambia's Opaque Non-Paris Club Borrowing
events.description: A wave of borrowing from Chinese state-linked lenders and commodity-backed loans was not fully captured in earlier debt statistics, complicating Zambia's 2020 default and the debt restructuring negotiations that followed under the G20 Common Framework.

events.title: The Transparency Pushback
events.description: The G20 Common Framework and updated DSA guidance began pushing for loan-by-loan disclosure from both debtors and creditors, specifically because contingent and off-book liabilities had repeatedly blindsided official debt sustainability numbers.

body.text: A DSA is only as good as the debt data fed into it. State-owned enterprise debt, government guarantees, public-private-partnership liabilities, and off-book borrowing routinely sit outside the headline numbers a DSA is built on, and by the time they surface, they tend to surface all at once, during a crisis, rather than gradually.

children.text: Blind Spot 2: Growth Assumptions Bent by Political Pressure

The clearest documented case is Greece's original 2010 IMF program. The IMF's own Independent Evaluation Office later found that the DSA underlying that program rested on GDP growth and fiscal adjustment assumptions optimistic enough to avoid the politically explosive conclusion that Greek debt needed restructuring from day one. The program went ahead without debt relief, growth came in far below projections, and Greece needed a second, much larger program in 2012 that included Private Sector Involvement, a haircut on privately held Greek bonds worth roughly €200 billion, the largest sovereign debt restructuring in history at the time. The lesson generalises well beyond Greece: a DSA's baseline growth assumption is a forecast made by people with strong institutional and political incentives to avoid concluding that a program country needs restructuring, and it deserves exactly as much scepticism as any other analyst's growth call.

body.title: Stress-Test a Baseline Yourself
body.scenario: An IMF staff DSA for a country projects real GDP growth accelerating from 1.5% this year to 4% within three years, driven by 'planned structural reforms', while the country has averaged 1.8% growth over the last decade and has not yet passed any of the reforms cited.
body.prompt: As the analyst reviewing this DSA before recommending a position in the country's bonds, what specific question do you raise, and what would make you comfortable with the 4% assumption?
body.modelAnswer: The question is simple: what is actually different this time that justifies more than doubling the trend growth rate, and has any of it happened yet? A credible answer needs either reforms already legislated and showing early results in leading indicators, or a comparable country that delivered a similar acceleration off a similar base. Citing reforms that are merely 'planned' but not yet passed is exactly the kind of assumption that turned Greece's original DSA into a case study: the growth acceleration existed on a page, not in the data, and the debt path built on top of it did not survive contact with reality.

children.text: Blind Spot 3: One Threshold Can't Fit Every Currency Structure

body.caption: Same-looking debt ratios, very different outcomes

cells: Almost entirely yen-denominated, held domestically by banks, pension funds, and the Bank of Japan
No default; r has stayed below g for most of the last two decades, and a captive domestic investor base absorbs new issuance without foreign-currency rollover risk
Roughly half foreign-currency denominated, including commercial bonds held mostly by external investors
Defaulted in 2022; foreign-currency debt service could not be met once reserves ran low, regardless of the headline ratio
Large foreign-currency share, a weak domestic institutional investor base, a history of repeated defaults
Defaulted in 2020 at a ratio far below Japan's, reflecting weak market confidence and currency mismatch rather than the debt level itself
Almost entirely rupee-denominated, dominated by domestic banks, insurers, and provident funds under statutory holding requirements
No IMF program; the currency and investor-base structure is repeatedly cited by the IMF as a key mitigant to an otherwise elevated ratio

children.text: India has never been under an IMF-supported program, so the DSA that applies to it runs through the annual Article IV consultation rather than a program negotiation, and it is a MAC DSA given India's deep domestic capital market access. Recent Article IV reports have generally rated India's public debt as sustainable, resting heavily on the same point the table above makes: general government debt is overwhelmingly rupee-denominated, and statutory requirements that Indian banks and insurers hold government bonds create a captive domestic buyer base that has little to do with sentiment among external investors. That said, the IMF's own stress tests on India have not been uncontroversial. Its 2024 Article IV review modelled a severe, low-probability adverse scenario in which general government debt could approach 100% of GDP, a projection the Indian government publicly and pointedly disputed as unrealistic. Whichever side of that specific disagreement you land on, it is a clean live example of exactly the tension this lesson has been building toward: a mechanical stress test result versus a country's own view of its growth and fiscal trajectory, playing out in real time rather than in a textbook. The IMF has also repeatedly flagged contingent liabilities as India's real watch item: state-level power distribution company (DISCOM) losses, past bank recapitalisation needs, and food and fertiliser subsidy arrears that sit partly off the headline central government fiscal deficit.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Sri Lanka defaulted in 2022 at a debt-to-GDP ratio well below Japan's, which has carried a much higher ratio for two decades without incident. Based on this lesson, what is the single biggest structural reason for the difference?
options: Sri Lanka's government was simply less competent than Japan's
Japan's debt is almost entirely domestic-currency and domestically held, while a large share of Sri Lanka's was foreign-currency debt owed to external investors
Japan has a much lower debt-to-GDP ratio than Sri Lanka, so the comparison is not meaningful
Sri Lanka's population is smaller, so its debt burden per person is inherently less sustainable
body.explanation: Japan's debt sits almost entirely in yen, held by domestic banks, pension funds, and the Bank of Japan itself, so there is no foreign-currency rollover risk and no dependency on external investor sentiment. Sri Lanka carried a meaningful share of foreign-currency commercial debt held by external investors, so once its reserves fell, it could not meet a foreign-currency obligation the way Japan can effectively manage yen-denominated debt. Currency composition and investor base, not the raw debt ratio, is what a DSA has to weigh most carefully across very differently structured sovereigns.

children.text: Reading a DSA Annex Like a Professional

body.title: Before You Trust Any DSA's Headline Risk Rating
steps: Check the baseline growth assumption against the country's own 10-year trailing average; flag anything that assumes a meaningfully faster growth path without a specific, already-enacted reason
Look specifically for a contingent liability stress test, and check whether state-owned enterprise, PPP, and sub-national government debt are included in the headline debt stock or left out
Note the currency composition of the debt stock: the share owed in foreign currency versus domestic currency changes what a given debt ratio actually means

Identify who holds the debt: a captive domestic buyer base, such as banks, insurers, and pension funds under statutory requirements, behaves very differently from external investors who can exit in a rollover crisis
Read whether the final risk rating matches the mechanical signal from the thresholds, or whether staff judgment overrode it, and if so, why
Cross-check the DSA's debt data against independent sources, such as BIS or World Bank International Debt Statistics, if the country has any history of hidden or off-book borrowing

body.text: This lesson explains the IMF-World Bank Debt Sustainability Analysis methodology and its documented limitations for educational purposes. It is not investment advice, and it is not a comment on the current creditworthiness of any specific sovereign named here. Debt ratios, risk classifications, and framework calibrations are updated frequently; always check the IMF's or World Bank's current published DSA for a given country before relying on a specific figure.

points: A DSA rating is a baseline projection plus a standardised set of stress tests, growth, primary balance, interest rate, and contingent liability shocks, not a raw prediction of default

MAC DSA applies to market-access economies like India and produces a mechanical signal that IMF staff can override with judgment; LIC DSF applies to concessional borrowers and classifies external debt distress risk using a Composite Indicator
Contingent liabilities and off-book borrowing, as in Mozambique and Zambia, have repeatedly blindsided official DSA numbers, because a DSA is only as accurate as the debt data it is fed

Baseline growth assumptions can be politically bent, as documented in the IMF's own post-mortem on Greece's 2010 program; treat an optimistic growth assumption with the same scepticism you would apply to any other analyst's forecast

The same debt-to-GDP ratio means very different things depending on currency composition and investor base, which is why Japan sustains around 260% while Sri Lanka defaulted near 100% and Argentina near 60%
